# Annulus downsizing in valve-sparing aortic root replacement predicts aortic valve reoperation in children and young adults

**Authors:** Duc M Giao; Dominic P Recco; Matthew Schildmeier; Kimberlee Gauvreau; Pakaparn Kittichokechai; Gerald R Marx; Christopher W Baird; Pedro J del Nido; Sitaram M Emani

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Cardiac Surgery, Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Mass | bDepartment of Cardiac Surgery, Smidt Heart Institute, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, Calif | cDepartment of Cardiology, Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Mass

## Abstract

Valve-sparing root replacement effectively treats aortic root pathology in adults, but data in pediatric patients are limited. We analyzed the midterm outcomes of valve-sparing root replacement in children and adolescents to define the risk factors for reintervention.

From 2006 to 2023, 80 patients underwent valve-sparing root replacement at 15 [11-19] years; 31 had connective tissue disorders, and 34 had concomitant greater than mild regurgitation. The primary end points were postoperative aortic valve dysfunction and reintervention with secondary outcome of mortality. Root and graft diameters were compared using Cox regression to determine the effect of intraoperative sizing.

The reimplantation technique with straight-tube (n = 38) or Valsalva (n = 40) grafts was used in all patients (except n = 2 remodeling with straight-tube). Thirty-seven patients underwent concurrent valvuloplasty, and 62 patients underwent ascending aortic replacement. Two patients had more than mild regurgitation at discharge with no perioperative mortality. The most common complication was arrhythmia requiring medication (11%). At 3.6 [0.6-8.2] years follow-up, 4 patients died, 20 patients required reoperation (4 re-repairs, 16 replacements), and 13 patients developed more than mild regurgitation. At 12 years, freedom from death, reintervention, and recurrent regurgitation were 92.0% (80.0%-96.9%), 54.3% (36.1%-69.4%), and 48.7% (25.1%-68.7%). For every 0.1 decrease in ratio of graft size to preoperative annulus diameter, reintervention risk increased by 40% (hazard ratio, 1.40 [1.04-1.90], P = .028). A ratio of less than 1.05 maximized model discrimination (hazard ratio, 3.30 [1.15-9.50], C-index 0.68).

Valve-sparing root replacement is safe and effective for aortic root aneurysms in children and young adults. Early arrhythmias, recurrent regurgitation, and midterm reoperation remain concerns. Graft upsizing or leaflet modification should be considered if ratio of intended graft to preoperative diameter is less than 1.05. Preoperative imaging can guide appropriate graft selection and plication extent to mitigate reintervention risk associated with excessive downsizing.

Key Words: aortic surgery, cardiovascular surgery, congenital heart disease, reoperation risk factors, valve-sparing root replacement

## Abstract

*Figure: Freedom from AoV reoperation after VSRR in children.*

Excessive root downsizing during VSRR is associated with AoV reoperation. Graft upsizing or leaflet modification should be considered if ratio of intended graft to preoperative annulus diameter is less than 1.05.

Data on the durability of VSRR in the pediatric population remain limited, and risk factors predicting recurrent valve dysfunction and reoperation remain undefined. Prior studies have shown acceptable outcomes with VSRR in children and young adults with the reimplantation technique. Our study corroborates these findings and demonstrates that annulus downsizing predicts AoV reoperation.

Aortic root replacement addresses conditions affecting the aortic root and proximal ascending aorta, such as aneurysms, dissection, and endocarditis.1 Although rare in children, aortic root dilation often results from genetic connective tissue disorders or congenital heart disease.2,3 In pediatric patients, replacement aims to reduce risks of aneurysmal rupture and progressive aortic valve (AoV) incompetence leading to ventricular dysfunction. Valve-sparing root replacement (VSRR) with reimplantation is gaining traction due to advantages over homograft and composite graft techniques, offering durable root stabilization and preservation of native valve tissue.4 VSRR avoids issues related to anticoagulation and reduces risks of thromboembolism, endocarditis, and redilation. It is particularly compelling for children when AoV cusps are repairable, allowing valve preservation in a growing child, delaying or avoiding prosthetic valve replacement.5, 6, 7, 8

Despite promising outcomes, data on the durability of pediatric VSRR remain limited. The largest series to date reported an 88.5% freedom from reintervention at 5 years.9 Previous work demonstrated that VSRR combined with complex valve reconstruction can yield low mortality and acceptable structural valve deterioration rates, with 70.1% freedom from significant AoV dysfunction at 1 year. However, identifying predictive factors for complications remains challenging.9 One emerging concept involves graft sizing. Our prior findings suggest that excessive graft undersizing relative to the native annulus diameter can lead to structural valve deterioration. This may result from excessive leaflet tissue within a smaller root, causing lower effective height and cusp prolapse, leading to regurgitation and reintervention. In this modest cohort, we found that smaller graft-to-annulus diameter ratio was predictive of structural valve deterioration. Prior studies did not thoroughly evaluate this mechanism, prompting further investigation here.10,11

We hypothesized that greater annulus downsizing during VSRR would predict worse postoperative AoV outcomes. Thus, our primary aim was to assess the relationship between graft sizing and risk of recurrent valvular dysfunction and AoV reoperation in children and young adults. Improved understanding of these factors may guide intraoperative decision-making and enhance long-term outcomes after VSRR.

## Material and Methods

### Patient Selection

This study was approved by the Boston Children's Hospital Institutional Review Board (IRB-P00050471, approved 5/2/2022) with a waiver of individual consent. A single-center, retrospective review was performed on patients who underwent VSRR between April 2006 and April 2023. Of 88 initially identified patients, we focused on those receiving VSRR with prosthetic tube graft replacement of all native sinuses. Exclusions included root reduction or single-sinus replacement (3%, n = 3), isolated ascending aorta replacement (1%, n = 1), prior AoV replacement (1%, n = 1), and other reasons (3%, n = 3). In total, 80 patients undergoing initial VSRR were included for postoperative outcomes and risk factor analysis.

### Surgical Technique

Our operative technique for reimplantation VSRR has been previously detailed.10, 11, 12, 13 In brief, cardiopulmonary bypass with moderate hypothermia and antegrade blood cardioplegia was used for myocardial protection. In 98% of cases (78/80), root replacement was performed via the David-V approach using a straight-tube (n = 38) or Valsalva (n = 40) graft. In the remaining 2 cases, root remodeling was performed via the Yacoub approach using a straight-tube graft. In general, graft size was selected based on preoperative annulus diameter z-score and degree of aortic regurgitation (AR). If the annulus diameter z-score was more than 4 to 6 and there was central AR more than trivial, then a graft of approximately equivalent size to the annulus or slightly smaller was selected to facilitate an “auto-annuloplasty” and improve central leaflet coaptation. With either technique or graft type, the commissures were placed under modest tension when securing the tabs to the graft to ensure adequate coaptation and effective heights and prevent leaflet prolapse with pressurization. This maneuver is especially critical in cases of annular downsizing. AoV repair techniques varied based on underlying disease and surgeon preference. Mid-leaflet plication was often used to prevent prolapse and increase coaptation and effective heights in cases of disproportionate cusp free edge length relative to root diameter, especially with downsizing.

### Outcome Measures

Collected medical record data included demographics, cardiac diagnoses, preoperative echocardiography (ECHO) measurements (aortic root and left ventricle [LV] dimensions), prior cardiac procedures, operative details including valvuloplasty techniques, postoperative clinical status, and discharge and follow-up ECHO findings. The primary end point was to identify risk factors for recurrent valvular dysfunction or AoV reoperation after VSRR, focusing on intraoperative root downsizing (ratio of graft size over preoperative aortic diameter). Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit and hospital stay durations, mortality, and perioperative complications.

### Aortic Root and Left Ventricular Measurements

ECHO scans were reviewed to evaluate AoV function, proximal aortic dimensions, and LV characteristics pre- and postoperatively. A single pediatric sonographer (M.S.) performed all measurements. Aortic diameter was recorded at 4 sites: AoV annulus, aortic sinus, sinotubular junction, and ascending aorta. Inner lumen diameters were taken at all locations. Additional data included degree of AR and aortic stenosis, ejection fraction, end-diastolic volume (EDV), mass, and mass-to-volume ratio. Aortic and LV measurement z-scores were calculated based on body surface area using institutional regression models.14

### Mortality, Recurrent Aortic Regurgitation, and Reoperation

Mortality was recorded at discharge and latest follow-up. Recurrent AR was defined as more than mild AR after the initial VSRR. Three patients were excluded: Two had more than mild AR on postbypass ECHO, and 1 lacked postoperative ECHO data. Reoperation was defined as AoV repair or replacement after the initial surgery; only the first reoperation was analyzed. Procedures like pseudoaneurysm repair, bleeding exploration, mechanical support, effusion drainage, and pacemaker placement were recorded as complications, not reoperations. Of note, 37 patients (46%) underwent any aortic valvuloplasty approach that grouped leaflet and commissure techniques, annuloplasty, and “other” root procedures together. To assess whether reimplantation without leaflet manipulation worsens valve deterioration, patients undergoing cusp plication, thinning, augmentation, or resection (21%, n = 17) were excluded from the subanalysis evaluating graft size-to-preoperative diameter ratios. Otherwise, the full cohort was included in all analyses of primary and secondary outcomes.

### Statistical Analyses

Baseline characteristics, operative details, and outcomes were summarized as frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, or mean (±SD) or median (IQR) for continuous variables, with nonmissing counts reported. Freedom from mortality, recurrent AR, and reoperation were estimated by Kaplan–Meier analysis and compared using the log-rank test. Cox regression models assessed relationships among graft size-to-root diameter ratios, z-scores, and time to recurrent AR or AoV reoperation, with hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs reported. Model discrimination was evaluated using Harrell's c-index. Analyses were conducted with SAS statistical software (version 15.3; SAS Institute) or Stata (version 17, StataCorp).

## Results

### Preoperative Patient Characteristics and Echocardiographic Measurements

Patient baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Of 80 patients, 31 (39%) had connective tissue disorders (18 with Marfan syndrome, 12 with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, 1 with Ehlers-Danlos). The majority of the primary cardiac diagnoses were proximal aortic aneurysms (root [n = 53, 66%], ascending [n = 7, 9%], and combined root and ascending [n = 13, 16%]). Most patients had either no (n = 46, 58%) or solely regurgitative (n = 33, 41%) AoV pathology. Approximately 40% of patients had bicuspid (n = 27, 34%) or unicuspid (n = 4, 5%) AoV morphology. The small minority of patients underwent prior AoV valve surgery (n = 9, 11%) or catheter (n = 4, 5%) intervention. Preoperative ECHO measurements are shown in Table 2. Across all 4 predefined proximal aortic locations, aortic sinus diameter z-score was largest at 6.48 ± 3.39, and ascending aortic diameter z-score was smallest at 3.84 ± 3.84. Thirty-four patients (43%) had moderate or severe AR, and almost all had mild or less aortic stenosis (n = 79, 99%). Many patients displayed associated LV dilation (EDV z-score 3.54 ± 3.43).

### Operative Details

Age at surgery was 15 [11-19] years, with two-thirds of patients (n = 53, 66%) aged less than 18 years at the time of index operation. Surgical technique was reimplantation in all but 2 patients (n = 78, 97%). Half of patients received a straight-tube (n = 40) or Valsalva (n = 40) graft. Thirty-seven patients (46%) underwent concurrent aortic valvuloplasty, 62 patients (78%) underwent ascending aortic replacement, and 9 patients (11%) underwent aortic arch replacement. Of those patients who underwent aortic valvuloplasty, leaflet thinning (n = 12, 15%) or plication (n = 14, 18%), commissuroplasty or commissurotomy (n = 19, 24%), and annuloplasty (n = 12, 15%) were all performed in more than 10% of cases. Secondary procedures were performed in approximately half of patients (n = 42, 53%). Intraoperative postbypass ECHO demonstrated mild or less AR in all but 2 patients (3%). ### Postoperative and Follow-up Outcomes and Echocardiographic Measurements

Postoperative intensive care unit and hospital length of stays were 1.9 [1.7-3.1] days and 6.4 [5.4-8.4] days, respectively (Table 4). There were no deaths before discharge. Complications present in more than 10% of the cohort included arrhythmia requiring medication (n = 9, 11%) and other (n = 9, 11%). At the time of discharge, mean diameter z-score for all 4 proximal aortic locations was less than 2.0, ranging from 1.02 at the annulus to 1.80 at the sinotubular junction (Table 2). Almost all patients were discharged with none/trivial (n = 55, 69%) or mild (n = 23, 29%) AR, with only 2 (3%) with moderate. Other LV measurements remained in normal range (−2 <z-score <2) with a decrease in LV EDV z-score compared with preoperatively (1.44 ± 2.20 vs 3.54 ± 3.43).

Median time to latest follow-up was 3.6 [0.6-8.2] years. There were 4 deaths (5%), and 20 patients (25%) underwent AoV reoperation (4 [5%] re-repairs and 16 [20%] replacements) at a median of 511 [91-2041] days after VSRR. Of the 20 reoperations, 16 (80%) were performed for progressive AR. Of these 16 reoperations, 15 (94%) proceeded with replacements for intraoperative findings of leaflet: prolapse in 6 (40%), dehiscence in 4 (27%), thickening/calcification in 1 (7%), tear in 1 (7%), and unknown in 3 (20%) due to transcatheter replacement. One re-repair was performed in the setting of recurrent AR for leaflet dehiscence. Interestingly, in patients with connective tissue disorders, 4 of 6 (67%) reoperations were related to leaflet elongation and prolapse. Follow-up ECHO scans after hospital discharge were available for 62 patients (78%). Of these patients, approximately one-fifth (n = 13, 22%) developed more than mild AR and approximately 40% (n = 29) experienced more than mild AR or AoV reoperation. At 12 years postoperatively, freedom from death, AoV reoperation, and recurrent AR were 92.0% (95% CI, 80.0-96.9), 54.3% (95% CI, 36.1-69.4), and 48.7% (95% CI, 25.1-68.7), respectively (Figure 1), and freedom from the composite outcome of AoV reoperation or AR recurrence was 30.7% (95% CI, 14.4-48.7). When stratified by graft type (straight-tube vs Valsalva), freedom from death was higher in the Valsalva group (100% vs 82.7% [95% CI, 60.2-93.2], P = .026) at 12 years after surgery (Figure E1). However, freedom from reoperation (P = .81), recurrent AR (P = .86), and composite outcome (P = .98) were all similar. Examining the 4 deaths, 1 patient died of arrythmia precipitated by dehydration in the setting of viral gastroenteritis, 1 patient died of acute respiratory failure secondary to a viral respiratory tract infection, and 2 patients died of unknown causes (no records available). The choice of graft is mostly dictated by surgeon preference rather than era or patient selection, and proposal of a driver for the association between type and survival would be speculative especially because the known causes of death are not directly related to the graft type used. Of note, 5 patients (6%) required reoperation for pseudoaneurysm development during follow-up. The pseudoaneurysms formed at the LV outflow tract subannular sutures in 3 patients, proximal hemostatic suture line at the base of the sinus in 1 patient, and right coronary button reimplantation site in 1 patient. On follow-up ECHO, diameter z-scores remained stable at all 4 proximal aortic locations, with the largest increase of 0.49 at the annulus (1.02 ± 2.46 vs 1.51 ± 2.65) (Table 2). However, mean diameter z-scores at all 4 segments remained between 1.32 and 1.51. Other LV measurement z-scores remained stable when compared with at discharge with an increase in LV EDV to 2.51 ± 2.63 from 1.44 ± 2.20.

### Factors Associated With Recurrent Regurgitation and Reoperation

Potential risk factors for reoperation, recurrent AR, or composite are shown in Table E1. No demographic factors were associated with a statistically higher risk of any of the outcomes of interest. Risk of the composite outcome after surgery was significantly higher in patients who had preoperative AR more than mild (HR, 2.74, 95% CI, 1.29-5.86, P = .009). Preoperative ECHO measurements were extensively evaluated as risk factors for all 3 primary end points. We analyzed absolute diameters and diameter z-scores at each of the 4 proximal aortic locations independently and as a ratio of selected graft size (Tables 5, E2, and E3). Sixty-one patients were included in sub-analysis of the ratio of graft diameter to preoperative AoV annulus diameter (excluded n = 2 for missing ECHO data and n = 17 as described in “Material and Methods”). Thirty-nine patients (64%) underwent graft “upsizing” (defined as ratio >1.05), 10 patients (16%) underwent graft “matching” (ratio 0.95-1.05), and 12 patients (20%) underwent graft “downsizing.” For downsized patients, mean annular diameter was 2.5 z-scores larger than for the entire cohort (6.61 ± 2.42 vs 4.10 ± 3.24) and preoperative more than mild AR was present in 6 patients (50%) compared with 43%. For every 1-cm increase in preoperative annulus diameter, there is 2.69 times higher risk of AoV reoperation (HR, 2.69, 95% CI, 1.29-5.58, P = .008). More clinically relevant, for every 0.1 decrease in the ratio of graft size-to-preoperative annulus diameter, the risk of AoV reoperation increased by 40% (HR, 1.40, 95% CI, 1.04-1.90, P = .028). A ratio of less than 1.05 maximized model discrimination (HR, 3.30, 95% CI, 1.15-9.50, P = .027, C-index 0.68). No other preoperative aortic segment sizes or ratios were associated.

## Discussion

Data remain relatively limited on the outcomes of VSRR in children with aortic root aneurysms or risk factors associated with repair failure. We previously reported our short-term experience with VSSR and remodeling with complex AoV reconstruction in pediatric patients.10 All 34 patients had more than mild preoperative AR and underwent concurrent AoV repair. During short-term follow-up (4.2 months), there were 5 reoperations for AoV replacement, and 2 patients presented with more than mild AR. Higher rates of structural valve deterioration (composite of AoV reoperation or more than mild AR) were noted with reimplantation technique; however, data suggested this to be due to a technical issue with graft sizing. On further evaluation, a more severe degree of preoperative AR and smaller graft-to-aortic annulus ratio were predictors of the primary outcome. Results were humbling because aortic root reconstruction with AoV repair demonstrated freedom from structural valve deterioration of 70% at 1 year but encouraging due to low operative risk and relatively successful valve preservation.

We sought to evaluate the midterm outcomes of VSRR via reimplantation in children and young adults at our institution and further investigate risk factors for postoperative failure, specifically, AoV reoperation, recurrent more than mild AR, and a composite of these 2 end points (Figure 2). Immediate outcomes were excellent. Hospital length of stay was 6.4 days, and there were no deaths. However, morbidity was moderate with approximately 30% of patients experiencing at least 1 complication. Most notable, 20% of patients developed arrhythmia requiring medical therapy or permanent pacemaker placement. Only 2 patients were discharged with more than mild AR, from 43% preoperative, and an associated correction of LV dilation was demonstrated with a decrease in EDV z-score from 3.5 to 1.4 at discharge.

*Figure 2: Graphical abstract.*

At 3.6 years follow-up, 4 patients died and 5 patients underwent reoperation for pseudoaneurysm development. From discharge, 11 more patients developed more than mild AR, resulting in a total of 13 patients (21%) with moderate or severe AR at follow-up. These findings were also reflected in recurrent trivial-to-mild LV dilation. Furthermore, AoV reintervention was required in 25% of patients. For the composite outcome, approximately 40% of patients experienced either more than mild AR or AoV reoperation at intermediate follow-up. Over time, aortic root dimensions remained within normal limits, suggesting durability of root stabilization with VSRR. On survival analysis, at 12 years postoperatively, freedom from death, AoV reoperation, recurrent more than mild AR, and composite were 92%, 54%, 49%, and 31%, respectively. On evaluation of risk factors, we noted an association between preoperative AR and the composite outcome, with a 2.74 times risk with more than mild AR. We identified larger preoperative annulus size as a predictor of AoV reoperation (2.69 times risk for every 1-cm increase in diameter). When excluding patients with AoV leaflet valvuloplasty, for every 0.1 decrease in ratio of graft size-to-preoperative annulus diameter, risk of AoV reoperation increased by 40% and a ratio of less than 1.05 maximized model discrimination. Although preoperative patient anatomy is rather nonmodifiable, based on these data, the surgeon should consider graft upsizing if the ratio of intended graft to preoperative annulus diameter is less than 1.05. The ratio of 1.05 likely reflects the difference between the inner lumen and outer tissue diameters given that the aortic wall at the annulus in placed within the graft. A target ratio slightly larger than 1.0 suggests that the best valve performance and durability are achieved when the graft is the “right-size” to accommodate the preoperative annular dimensions. On the other hand, if annular downsizing is deemed appropriate, the surgeon could consider leaflet modification (eg, plication, resection) to restore normal aortic root complex proportions. Caution should be used when universally performing an isolated VSRR reimplantation technique because the native leaflets are commonly disproportional to the intended reconstructed root dimensions and may lead to higher rates of AoV reintervention.

The largest study on VSRR in children was reported by Fraser and colleagues.9 Technically, they showed favorable early outcomes with remodeling techniques (Yacoub/David-II) for valve preservation. However, a trend toward postoperative late annular dilatation and AR requiring AoV replacement led to abandonment of this technique and use of the modified David-V reimplantation strategy using a Valsalva graft. From 1997 to 2017, 100 pediatric valve-sparing aortic root procedures were performed. Compared with the index study, age at operation was similar (14 vs 15 years) and most patients underwent reimplantation procedures (84% vs 97%), although a higher percentage of patients had connective tissue disorders (90% vs 39%). Six patients required late reintervention for development of pseudoaneurysms. Reintervention-free recurrent AR was not reported. Of the 84 patients undergoing a reimplantation procedure, freedom from reintervention at 10 years was 79%. We report a freedom from AoV reoperation of 54% at 12 years. Although our results may appear less acceptable, there are several explanations for such. Our group had a significantly higher rate of nontricuspid AoV anatomy (39% vs 12%), preoperative more than mild AR (43% vs 7%), and concurrent AoV repair (46% vs 9%). In this context, our results are rather comparable. Furthermore, our rates of recurrent AR and AoV reoperation are similar to other prior studies evaluating results of VSRR in children that report 10-year freedom from such outcomes between 53% and 68%.15, 16, 17

Although the results of VSRR in children described in this article and by others are acceptable, they are far worse than those reported in adults. Freedom from postoperative more than mild AR is reported at approximately 75% at 10 years, and freedom from reintervention for AoV disease is between 88% and 93%.18,19 This difference is partially due to the difficulties with repair of congenital AoV disease and higher rates of complex AoV repair at the time of VSRR. However, we anticipate that surgical planning for aortic root reconstruction will ultimately provide the patient with the best possible long-term outcome. Our institution has begun using preoperative 3-dimensional modeling and simple analytical models to assist surgeons in selecting the appropriate graft size and degree of intraoperative leaflet modification to prevent AoV reintervention due to associated risk with over-downsizing.20 Furthermore, intraoperative conduction mapping at our institution has been successfully performed in 149 patients undergoing complex biventricular repair with a median mapping time of 6 minutes, identification of the His bundle in 97% of cases, and significantly reduced postoperative atrioventricular block and pacemaker frequency in select populations.21 This technique is now being used with VSRR given the high arrythmia burden demonstrated. We anticipate similar benefits as shown in patients undergoing biventricular repair and plan to create a predictive model of conduction anatomy for centers without such technology available.

### Limitations

This study is limited by its retrospective nature in a single-center institution. The timeframe spanned across 2 decades, and changes in management may have influenced our outcomes. Additionally, incomplete data were collected for some of the ECHO measurements due to poor acoustic windows or insufficient imaging of target anatomy. Our analyses were limited by modest sample sizes, even if this represents one of the largest populations of VSRR and complex AoV repair procedures in children.

## Conclusions

VSRR is a safe and effective option for children and young adults with aortic root aneurysms and provides an alternative strategy to composite root replacement with avoidance of potential complications of valve prostheses. However, early arrhythmias and late recurrent AR and AoV reintervention remain concerns. Adequate graft sizing is critical for the durability of repair, and undersizing should be avoided to prevent AoV reoperation. Graft upsizing or leaflet modification should be considered if the ratio of intended graft to preoperative annulus diameter is less than 1.05.
